families.name: Britpop and the last rock hits

genres.name: The Beatles: Rubber Soul
genres.text: On 3 December 1965 the Beatles released Rubber Soul. Until then, albums were often a few hits padded out with filler. Rubber Soul held only new songs, all written by the band, and the record sounded like a whole, with a sitar in Norwegian Wood and thoughtful lyrics. In Britain no single was even taken from it. Pop musicians began to see the album as something to listen to from start to finish.
genres.listen: In Norwegian Wood, George Harrison plays sitar, an Indian string instrument. Listen to how the little melody of the sitar follows the vocal.

genres.name: The Beach Boys: Pet Sounds
genres.text: On 16 May 1966 the Beach Boys released Pet Sounds. Brian Wilson had stopped touring and stayed in the studio in Los Angeles, where he worked with the best session musicians. He used bicycle bells, a kind of theremin, strings and barking dogs. Wilson had heard Rubber Soul and wanted to make something better. Paul McCartney later called Pet Sounds his favourite album and an inspiration for Sgt. Pepper.
genres.listen: God Only Knows begins with a horn and a harpsichord. Listen to how the voices sing over one another in a round at the end.

genres.name: The Doors: The Doors
genres.text: On 4 January 1967 the first album by The Doors, from Los Angeles, was released. In 1966 the band had been the house band at the club Whisky a Go Go. They were fired there for a shocking version of The End, but also discovered by label boss Jac Holzman. Ray Manzarek's organ and Jim Morrison's dark lyrics made the record unlike anything else. Light My Fire became a number 1 hit.
genres.listen: In Light My Fire, listen for the long organ and guitar solos in the middle. For the hit single, most of them were cut out.

tracks.title: Break On Through (To the Other Side)

genres.name: The Velvet Underground & Nico
genres.text: In March 1967 The Velvet Underground & Nico was released, with a sleeve by the artist Andy Warhol: a banana you could peel. Lou Reed sang about drugs and the dark side of New York, and John Cale played electric viola, as he had learned to do in the avant-garde. At first the album sold almost nothing. Later it became one of the most influential rock records ever, for punk, post-punk and alternative rock.
genres.listen: In Venus in Furs, John Cale plays electric viola: a grating drone full of dissonance, from the avant-garde.

genres.name: Jimi Hendrix: Purple Haze
genres.text: In 1966 the American guitarist Jimi Hendrix came to London and formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience there with two British musicians. Purple Haze was released on 17 March 1967. Hendrix used distortion and feedback as a sound, not as a mistake. British guitarists such as Eric Clapton and Jeff Beck came to watch and were impressed. In June 1967 he played at the Monterey Pop Festival and became a star in America too.
genres.listen: The intro begins with a tritone, the interval once known as the devil's interval. Then comes the Hendrix chord, E7#9.

genres.name: Album rock on FM radio
genres.text: On 7 April 1967, DJ Tom Donahue began a programme on the small FM station KMPX in San Francisco in which he played whole album sides instead of just hits. The FM band had better sound quality and few listeners, so there was room to experiment. More and more stations followed. Later the format was named album-oriented rock, AOR. A song no longer had to fit into three minutes.
genres.listen: On the album, Light My Fire by The Doors lasts more than seven minutes, with long organ and guitar solos. AM radio played a shortened version, FM often the whole thing.

genres.name: The Beatles: Sgt. Pepper
genres.text: On 26 May 1967 Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band was released in Britain. The Beatles pretended to be a different band, and the songs run into one another. The sleeve shows dozens of famous people, and as the first rock album it had all the lyrics on the back. Many people saw it as the first album meant as a work of art. It became one of the best-selling albums of the 1960s.
genres.listen: A Day in the Life ends with an orchestra sliding from low to high, followed by one long piano chord that rings on for more than forty seconds.

tracks.title: Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds
Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band

genres.name: Pink Floyd: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
genres.text: On 4 August 1967 the first album by Pink Floyd was released. The band played in London clubs such as the UFO, where light shows were projected onto the musicians. Guitarist and singer Syd Barrett wrote strange, fairy-tale songs and long improvisations. Drugs soon got him into trouble; in 1968 he was replaced by David Gilmour. Pink Floyd grew into one of the biggest album bands ever.
genres.listen: Astronomy Domine opens the album. Listen to the strange, shifting chords and the echo on the guitar.

genres.name: Rolling Stone
genres.text: On 9 November 1967 the first issue of Rolling Stone appeared in San Francisco, a magazine started by 21-year-old Jann Wenner. It wrote seriously about rock music, with long interviews and album reviews. This made rock something to think and talk about, like film or literature. What Rolling Stone wrote about an album could decide whether it succeeded.
genres.listen: The magazine takes its name from Rollin' Stone by Muddy Waters, as do the Rolling Stones. Listen to how the old blues song and Like a Rolling Stone by Bob Dylan are both about drifting from place to place.

genres.name: The Band: Music from Big Pink
genres.text: On 1 July 1968 Music from Big Pink was released by The Band, Bob Dylan's backing group. Part of it was made in Big Pink, a pink house in New York State. Where much rock was loud and psychedelic, this record sounded calm, with country, gospel and folk. Eric Clapton said this album persuaded him to quit Cream. It is seen as a beginning of Americana, rock with old American roots.
genres.listen: In The Weight, listen to how the singers take turns from verse to verse. It sounds like a group of friends playing together in a room.

genres.name: Led Zeppelin
genres.text: On 12 January 1969 the first album by Led Zeppelin was released in America, the band of guitarist Jimmy Page and singer Robert Plant. They played the blues harder and heavier than ever, with long guitar solos and the pounding drums of John Bonham. In Britain Led Zeppelin almost never released singles: they sold albums and played long concerts. They became one of the best-selling bands ever.
genres.listen: Dazed and Confused is slow and heavy. Listen to how Page draws a violin bow across his guitar in the middle section.

genres.name: The Who: Tommy
genres.text: On 23 May 1969 Tommy by The Who was released, a double album that tells one story: about a deaf, dumb and blind boy who becomes a pinball champion and a kind of messiah. Guitarist Pete Townshend called it a rock opera. The Who played the whole album live, at Woodstock among other places. Later it became a film and a musical. A rock album could now tell a long story.
genres.listen: Pinball Wizard begins with fast chords on an acoustic guitar. Then the band joins in, like a pinball machine starting to rattle.

genres.name: Creedence Clearwater Revival: Green River
genres.text: On 7 August 1969 Green River by Creedence Clearwater Revival, from California, was released. Singer and guitarist John Fogerty wrote almost all the songs and produced the record himself. The band sounded like a group from the swamps of the American South, with short, tight songs. That style is called swamp rock. The album reached number 1 in the United States, and Bad Moon Rising and Green River both reached number two.
genres.listen: In Green River, listen for the short, twangy guitar riff at the start. With no solos or long sections, the song lasts less than three minutes.

genres.name: Woodstock
genres.text: From 15 to 18 August 1969, almost half a million people came to a field near Bethel in New York State. At the Woodstock festival, Santana, Joe Cocker, Creedence Clearwater Revival and The Who played, among others. Jimi Hendrix closed on Monday morning. Through the film Woodstock and the triple album of 1970, the festival became a famous symbol of the youth culture of the 1960s.
genres.listen: Listen to how Hendrix plays the American national anthem with feedback, the howling sound of a guitar close to the amplifier. Many listeners heard the bombs and sirens of the Vietnam War in it.

tracks.title: The Star Spangled Banner (Live at Woodstock)
With a Little Help from My Friends (Live at Woodstock)

genres.name: King Crimson: In the Court of the Crimson King
genres.text: On 10 October 1969 the first album by King Crimson was released. The band mixed rock with jazz, classical music and long instrumental pieces, with a Mellotron that sounds like a choir or an orchestra. The album is often seen as the beginning of progressive rock, prog for short: rock with the ambition of classical music. The sleeve shows a screaming face, painted by a friend of the band.
genres.listen: 21st Century Schizoid Man starts softly and then breaks loose, with distorted vocals, saxophones and fast, complicated unison runs.

tracks.title: In the Court of the Crimson King

genres.name: Black Sabbath
genres.text: On Friday 13 February 1970 the first album by Black Sabbath was released, from Birmingham, an industrial city in England. Guitarist Tony Iommi had lost two fingertips in a factory accident and played with homemade caps on his fingers. His slow, heavy riffs gave a dark sound. Ozzy Osbourne sang about fear and evil. Black Sabbath is often seen as the first heavy metal band.
genres.listen: The title song begins with rain, thunder and a church bell. Then comes the riff, with the tritone, the devil's interval.

genres.name: Neil Young: Southern Man
genres.text: On 19 September 1970 After the Gold Rush by the Canadian singer Neil Young was released. On the song Southern Man he condemned the racism and slavery of the southern United States. He did so again two years later with Alabama. Young played both gentle folk and hard guitar rock, and later became a model for grunge bands. His songs provoked a well-known answer from the South.
genres.listen: In Southern Man you hear Young's sharp, distorted electric guitar above the piano. The lyrics are an accusation.

tracks.title: Only Love Can Break Your Heart

genres.name: Led Zeppelin IV
genres.text: On 8 November 1971 the fourth album by Led Zeppelin was released, with no title and no band name on the sleeve. It became one of the best-selling albums ever. Stairway to Heaven, more than eight minutes long, became the most requested song on American FM radio, even though it was never released as a single in America. Anyone who wanted the song had to buy the album.
genres.listen: Stairway to Heaven begins with an acoustic guitar, soon joined by recorders, and builds over eight minutes to a hard rock climax.

genres.name: David Bowie: Ziggy Stardust
genres.text: On 16 June 1972 The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars by David Bowie was released. He invented a character, a rock star from space, and became that character, on stage and off, with make-up and glitter costumes. The album tells of Ziggy's rise and fall. On 3 July 1973 Bowie let Ziggy die on stage in London. Rock could now be theatre too.
genres.listen: Starman is about an alien who wants to meet the children of Earth. Listen to the chorus, which recalls Somewhere Over the Rainbow.

genres.name: NEU! and krautrock
genres.text: In 1972 the first album by NEU! was released, a duo from Düsseldorf: Michael Rother and Klaus Dinger, who had earlier played with Kraftwerk. Dinger played a tight, straight-ahead rhythm, the motorik beat, which stayed the same for minutes on end. British journalists called such German bands krautrock. Bowie, Brian Eno, Joy Division and later Radiohead drew inspiration from it.
genres.listen: Hallogallo lasts ten minutes in a steady 4/4 time, in which the drum rhythm hardly changes. Listen to how the rhythm carries you along like a car on the motorway.

genres.name: Yes: Close to the Edge
genres.text: On 8 September 1972 Close to the Edge by Yes was released. The title song lasts almost nineteen minutes and takes up a whole album side, with sections like those of a classical piece. Keyboard player Rick Wakeman played organ, Mellotron and Moog. Prog bands such as Yes, Genesis and Emerson, Lake & Palmer filled stadiums with long, complicated pieces. Exactly that was what punk would ridicule a few years later.
genres.listen: The song begins with birdsong and a chaotic explosion of guitar and organ, and only then settles down.

genres.name: Pink Floyd: The Dark Side of the Moon
genres.text: On 1 March 1973 The Dark Side of the Moon by Pink Floyd was released in America. The album is about time, money, war and madness, and the songs run into one another. The band used synthesizers, tape loops and the voices of people from the studio. The sleeve with a prism became one of the best known ever. The album stayed on the American album chart for years, more than 900 weeks in total.
genres.listen: Money is in 7/4 time. Count along: the rhythm comes from a tape loop with cash register sounds and jingling coins.

tracks.title: The Great Gig in the Sky

genres.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd: Sweet Home Alabama
genres.text: In June 1974 Sweet Home Alabama by Lynyrd Skynyrd, from Jacksonville, was released, an answer to Southern Man and Alabama by Neil Young. The band took the side of the South, although the lyrics are ambiguous. Lynyrd Skynyrd was the best-known example of southern rock: blues, country and hard rock, with three guitarists. Young and the band, incidentally, respected each other. In 1977 three band members died in a plane crash.
genres.listen: The riff is D, C, G. The C is the flattened seventh of D, which makes it sound Mixolydian, as is common in blues and country.

genres.name: Bruce Springsteen: Born to Run
genres.text: On 25 August 1975 Born to Run by Bruce Springsteen, from New Jersey, was released. He worked on it for months and wanted it to sound like the big productions of Phil Spector, with saxophone, glockenspiel and strings. The songs are about young people from small towns who want to escape. Springsteen appeared on the covers of Time and Newsweek at the same time. His three-hour concerts later made him a stadium star.
genres.listen: Listen to the wall of sound in Born to Run: guitars, saxophone, glockenspiel and lyrics that cry out to get away.

genres.name: Queen: Bohemian Rhapsody
genres.text: On 31 October 1975 Bohemian Rhapsody by Queen was released, from the album A Night at the Opera. The song begins as a ballad, moves into an opera section for which the voices were recorded some 180 times over one another, then turns into hard rock and ends quietly. It has no chorus, and it lasts almost six minutes. Even so, it stayed at number one in Britain for nine weeks. The video helped usher in the era of the music video.
genres.listen: Count the sections: ballad, opera, hard rock, ending. In the opera section, listen to how the voices jump from left to right.

genres.name: Frampton Comes Alive!
genres.text: On 6 January 1976 Frampton Comes Alive! was released, a double live record by the British guitarist Peter Frampton. It became the best-selling album of 1976 in America and one of the best-selling live records ever. Frampton made his guitar talk with a talk box, a small tube with which you shape the sound in your mouth. In those years rock became a big industry, with stadiums, tours and albums that sold millions.
genres.listen: In Show Me the Way you hear the talk box: the guitar seems to sing words. The audience cheers as it begins.

tracks.title: Do You Feel Like We Do

genres.name: Ramones
genres.text: On 23 April 1976 the first album by the Ramones, from Queens in New York, was released. Fourteen songs in less than thirty minutes, with three chords, fast and loud. They played at the club CBGB, as did Patti Smith and Talking Heads. After the long solos of prog and the expensive stadium shows, punk said: anyone can do this. In July 1976 the Ramones played in London, and young Britons began starting bands of their own.
genres.listen: Blitzkrieg Bop begins with the chanted Hey! Ho! Let's go!. The song lasts just over two minutes and has hardly any solo.

genres.name: Sex Pistols: Anarchy in the U.K.
genres.text: On 26 November 1976 Anarchy in the U.K., the first single by the Sex Pistols, was released. Manager Malcolm McLaren had brought singer Johnny Rotten into the band. On 1 December the band swore at the presenter Bill Grundy live on television. The next day it was on every front page. Concerts were cancelled and the record label dropped the band. Punk was now a scandal across all of Britain.
genres.listen: Listen to the wall of double-tracked guitars and the sneering, half sung, half shouted voice of Johnny Rotten.

genres.name: Fleetwood Mac: Rumours
genres.text: On 4 February 1977 Rumours by Fleetwood Mac was released. During the recording, two couples in the band split up, and they sang about each other in the songs. The album became one of the best-selling albums ever. The sound was smooth and polished: perfect vocals, clear guitars and a tight rhythm section. This kind of big, expensive rock was exactly what punk rebelled against.
genres.listen: In Go Your Own Way, Lindsey Buckingham sings to his ex, Stevie Nicks, who sings along in the backing vocals.

genres.name: Talking Heads: 77
genres.text: On 16 September 1977 the first album by Talking Heads was released. The band played at CBGB, but sounded very different from the Ramones: nervous, clever and danceable. Singer David Byrne and the others had met at art school. Bassist Tina Weymouth played bare, tight bass lines. In the 1980s they turned more and more to funk and African rhythms.
genres.listen: Psycho Killer runs on a bare bass line around the note A. Part of the lyrics is in French.

genres.name: Steely Dan: Aja
genres.text: On 23 September 1977 Aja by Steely Dan, the duo of Walter Becker and Donald Fagen, was released. They used jazz chords in pop songs and had the best session musicians of Los Angeles and New York play the same part over and over, until it was perfect. The album became their best seller. Its sound later became a benchmark for testing hi-fi equipment.
genres.listen: In Peg you hear so-called mu chords, with an added second. Listen also to the guitar solo, for which seven guitarists were tried.

genres.name: The Rolling Stones: Miss You
genres.text: In May 1978 Miss You by the Rolling Stones was released, with a disco bass and a tight beat. The Stones went along with the music heard in the clubs, and the song became a number one in America. For some rock fans it felt like betrayal. A year later in Chicago, disco records were blown up at Disco Demolition Night. Did rock have to adapt to what was popular?
genres.listen: Listen to the bass skipping with octave jumps, the harmonica and Mick Jagger singing in falsetto.

genres.name: Joy Division: Unknown Pleasures
genres.text: On 15 June 1979 Unknown Pleasures by Joy Division, from Manchester, was released on the small label Factory. Producer Martin Hannett made the sound cool and spacious, with dry drums and a lot of reverb. The sleeve shows white lines on black: the signals of a pulsar from an astronomy book. After punk came post-punk: darker, slower and more experimental. Singer Ian Curtis died in May 1980.
genres.listen: In She's Lost Control the drums sound almost mechanical, and Peter Hook's bass plays the melody.

genres.name: The Clash: London Calling
genres.text: On 14 December 1979 London Calling by The Clash was released in Britain, a double album for the price of one. The band had started as a punk band, but now mixed punk with reggae, ska, rockabilly, jazz and soul. The sleeve, with bassist Paul Simonon smashing his bass guitar, refers to the sleeve of Elvis's first album. Punk turned out not to be a fixed style, but an attitude.
genres.listen: In the title song, Joe Strummer's voice sounds like an emergency message on the radio, about a looming disaster.

genres.name: The Cure and gothic
genres.text: On 8 April 1980 A Forest by The Cure, the band of singer Robert Smith, was released. The guitar sounds through a flanger, an effect that makes the tone slowly drift, the bass plays the same motif over and over, and everything bathes in reverb. The song is about someone who follows a voice in a forest and gets lost. Smith's black clothes and tangled hair became the uniform of a new youth culture: the goths.
genres.listen: Listen to the floating guitar with flanger and the bass that keeps playing the same motif, like someone walking in circles in the forest.

genres.name: Iron Maiden and the NWOBHM
genres.text: On 14 April 1980 the first album by Iron Maiden, from East London, was released. They belonged to the New Wave of British Heavy Metal: young bands who played metal faster and rougher, with the energy of punk. Iron Maiden had two guitarists who played melodies together, and a monster as mascot on every sleeve, Eddie. American bands such as Metallica learned a lot from them.
genres.listen: In Running Free you hear the fast, galloping bass of Steve Harris and the raw voice of singer Paul Di'Anno.

genres.name: Queen: Another One Bites the Dust
genres.text: In August 1980 Another One Bites the Dust by Queen was released. Bassist John Deacon wrote the bass riff, inspired by the disco group Chic. On the advice of Michael Jackson they released it as a single. The song went to number one in America and was also played on Black radio stations. A stadium band had a funk hit, and not every rock fan was happy about it.
genres.listen: The bass riff recalls Good Times by Chic. Listen also to the sounds played backwards.

genres.name: Toto: Africa
genres.text: In April 1982 Toto IV was released, with Africa and Rosanna. Toto consisted of session musicians from Los Angeles who also played on other people's records, including Thriller by Michael Jackson. Their sound was smooth, perfect and complicated. Critics found it soulless, but the album won six Grammys. Years later, through the internet, Africa became one of the best-known songs of the 1980s.
genres.listen: Africa has a rhythm of percussion and a synthesizer melody that sounds like a kalimba. Listen to the big, multi-voice chorus.

genres.name: R.E.M.: Murmur
genres.text: On 12 April 1983 Murmur, the first album by R.E.M. from the student town of Athens in Georgia, was released. Michael Stipe sang in a mumble, with lyrics you could half make out, and guitarist Peter Buck played chiming chords. The band grew big through student radio stations and small venues, outside MTV. This is how college rock arose, later called alternative rock: rock for those who found stadiums too big.
genres.listen: In Radio Free Europe you hear the chiming guitar and Stipe's voice, which you can hardly make out.

genres.name: Metallica: Kill 'Em All
genres.text: On 25 July 1983 Kill 'Em All, the first album by Metallica from California, was released by a small label. The band played faster and harder than the hard rock on the radio: thrash metal. They had listened closely to British bands such as Iron Maiden and Motörhead. Metallica first spread its music on cassettes that fans copied among themselves. Ten years later they filled stadiums.
genres.listen: In Seek & Destroy, listen for the riff that keeps coming back and Lars Ulrich's fast, tight drums.

genres.name: Van Halen: Jump
genres.text: At the end of 1983 Jump by Van Halen was released, the band of guitarist Eddie Van Halen, one of the most influential guitarists of his time. He, of all people, played the riff of Jump on a synthesizer, an Oberheim, instead of on the guitar. For some of the fans that was betrayal. Jump became the band's biggest hit, and their only number one in America. The same question again: adapt or stay true?
genres.listen: The riff does not come from the guitar, but from the Oberheim synthesizer. Only in the middle comes the short, lightning-fast guitar solo.

genres.name: Dire Straits and the CD
genres.text: In May 1985 Brothers in Arms by Dire Straits, the band of guitarist Mark Knopfler, was released. It was one of the first fully digitally recorded albums and one of the first albums to sell better on CD than on vinyl. Many people bought a CD player for it. The video of Money for Nothing, with computer animation, was in 1987 the first to be broadcast by MTV Europe.
genres.listen: In Money for Nothing, Sting sings I want my MTV. Listen to Knopfler's fat guitar riff, played with a wah-wah pedal that stayed in one position.

genres.name: Bon Jovi and hair metal
genres.text: On 18 August 1986 Slippery When Wet by Bon Jovi, from New Jersey, was released. The band sounded like hard rock, but with pop melodies and big choruses, and looked good on MTV, with backcombed hair. The album became one of the best-selling of the 1980s. Later this style was called hair metal. Livin' on a Prayer, about a young couple having a hard time, became an anthem at parties.
genres.listen: In Livin' on a Prayer you hear the talk box of guitarist Richie Sambora and a chorus that goes even higher after the key change.

tracks.title: You Give Love a Bad Name

genres.name: U2: The Joshua Tree
genres.text: On 9 March 1987 The Joshua Tree by U2, from Dublin, was released. The band had started in post-punk, but grew into a stadium band. Guitarist The Edge played with a lot of echo, so that a few notes sounded like a whole orchestra. The album was about America, faith and longing, and became their first number one in America. U2 became one of the biggest live acts of the 1980s and 1990s.
genres.listen: Where the Streets Have No Name begins with an organ and then The Edge's guitar, which, through the echo, sounds like a stream of notes.

tracks.title: Where the Streets Have No Name
I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For

genres.name: Guns N' Roses: Appetite for Destruction
genres.text: On 21 July 1987 Appetite for Destruction by Guns N' Roses, from Los Angeles, was released. After the glossy hair metal, this band sounded raw and dangerous again. At first the album sold badly, until MTV began playing the video of Welcome to the Jungle. It became the best-selling debut album in America. Slash's guitar lick in Sweet Child o' Mine began as a finger exercise.
genres.listen: Sweet Child o' Mine begins with Slash's famous lick. Axl Rose sings high and raw.

genres.name: Living Colour
genres.text: On 3 May 1988 Vivid by Living Colour, from New York, was released, a band of four Black musicians. They played funk metal: hard guitars with funk rhythms. Guitarist Vernon Reid had, together with others, founded the Black Rock Coalition, because Black rock musicians hardly got any chances with record companies. Rock came from Black music, but in the 1980s it was seen mainly as white music.
genres.listen: Cult of Personality begins with a speech by Malcolm X, and at the end you hear John F. Kennedy and Franklin D. Roosevelt. Listen to Vernon Reid's sharp guitar riff.

genres.name: Pixies: Doolittle
genres.text: On 17 April 1989 Doolittle by the Pixies, from Boston, was released. The band alternated soft verses with loud, screaming choruses, and singer Black Francis sang about strange and creepy things. Bassist Kim Deal often sang along. In America the album only reached number 98, in Britain number 8. Kurt Cobain later said that with Smells Like Teen Spirit he was trying to imitate the Pixies.
genres.listen: In Debaser you hear Kim Deal's driving bass and the singer screaming the chorus. Notice the switch between soft and hard.

genres.name: The Stone Roses
genres.text: On 2 May 1989 the debut album by The Stone Roses, from Manchester, was released. The band mixed guitar pop of the 1960s with the danceable rhythm of the house clubs. The band became the figurehead of Madchester, the music scene of that city. At first the album was not a big hit, but it grew into one of the most important British records. Bands such as Oasis later named The Stone Roses as a major example for their own Britpop.
genres.listen: Listen to how I Wanna Be Adored begins very softly with only a little bass line. Only after more than a minute does the singing join in.

genres.name: The first Lollapalooza
genres.text: On 18 July 1991 the first Lollapalooza began in Chandler, Arizona. Singer Perry Farrell devised it as the farewell tour of his band Jane's Addiction. It was a travelling festival that visited more than twenty cities. The programme included alternative rock, industrial from Nine Inch Nails and rap from Ice-T. Music that hardly got on the radio suddenly found a large audience. Soon afterwards grunge broke through.
genres.listen: In Been Caught Stealing, listen for a dog barking among the guitars. Jane's Addiction combined a funky rhythm with a strange, playful sound.

genres.name: Nirvana: Nevermind
genres.text: On 24 September 1991 Nevermind by Nirvana, from Seattle, was released. Smells Like Teen Spirit runs on four power chords, with quiet verses and loud choruses. The video, set in a gym with cheerleaders wearing anarchy symbols, was played endlessly on MTV. In January 1992 the album pushed Dangerous by Michael Jackson off the top spot. The glossy rock of the 1980s was suddenly old-fashioned.
genres.listen: Power chords have only a root and a fifth, with no third: they are neither major nor minor and sound good with a lot of distortion. Listen to the four chords.

genres.name: Soundgarden and grunge
genres.text: On 8 October 1991 Badmotorfinger by Soundgarden, also from Seattle, was released. The label Sub Pop brought together the bands of the city, and the press called the music grunge. Soundgarden mixed punk with the heavy riffs of Black Sabbath and Led Zeppelin, and singer Chris Cornell had a voice with a wide range. Together with Nirvana and Pearl Jam they made Seattle the rock capital of the world in a few months.
genres.listen: Jesus Christ Pose has a complicated rhythm and a guitar in drop-D tuning: the lowest string a whole tone lower, for a heavier sound.

genres.name: The Smashing Pumpkins: Siamese Dream
genres.text: On 27 July 1993 Siamese Dream by The Smashing Pumpkins, from Chicago, was released. Singer and guitarist Billy Corgan piled dozens of guitar parts on top of one another into a wall of sound. The songs shift between lovely and furious. The album was a great success and made the band one of the most important in alternative rock in the 1990s.
genres.listen: In Today a cheerful guitar motif plays, but the lyrics are about the best day of your life, while you actually want to die. Music and lyrics pull apart.

genres.name: Green Day: Dookie
genres.text: On 1 February 1994 Dookie by Green Day, from California, was released, their first album on a major record label. After grunge, punk came back, but with pop melodies and funny lyrics about boredom and doubt. Old punk fans at their home club found it a betrayal, but millions of teenagers bought the album. Punk became pop punk, and so bigger than ever.
genres.listen: In the verse of Basket Case you hear a chord sequence that also underlies Pachelbel's Canon. Listen to how fast and loud it still sounds.

genres.name: The death of Kurt Cobain
genres.text: In early April 1994 Kurt Cobain, the singer of Nirvana, took his own life in Seattle. He was 27. Cobain coped badly with fame and felt like a stranger in the music industry that had made him rich. His death affected millions of young people. Grunge lost its face, and in Britain bands deliberately looked the other way, towards their own pop history.
genres.listen: All Apologies sounds calm and acoustic on the album MTV Unplugged in New York, recorded in November 1993. It was only released after his death.

tracks.title: The Man Who Sold the World
Where Did You Sleep Last Night

genres.name: Blur versus Oasis
genres.text: On 14 August 1995 Blur from London and Oasis from Manchester released a single on the same day, and the media turned it into the Battle of Britpop. Blur won the chart, but Oasis won the world with (What's the Story) Morning Glory?. Britpop looked back to the Beatles, The Kinks and The Who, as an answer to American grunge. It was one of the last times two guitar bands made the news.
genres.listen: Wonderwall by Oasis revolves around an acoustic guitar with a capo, on which a few strings keep ringing open. That is why it sounds full and floating.

genres.name: Foo Fighters: The Colour and the Shape
genres.text: On 20 May 1997 The Colour and the Shape by Foo Fighters was released. After the death of Kurt Cobain, Nirvana drummer Dave Grohl had recorded a first album almost entirely alone. He made this second album with a full band, and Grohl sang and played guitar. Everlong became one of the best-known rock songs of the 1990s. Foo Fighters grew into one of the biggest stadium bands.
genres.listen: In Everlong, listen to how the fast guitars and drums in the chorus suddenly get very loud, after quieter verses.

genres.name: Radiohead: OK Computer
genres.text: On 16 June 1997 OK Computer by Radiohead, from near Oxford, was released in Britain. The album is about alienation in a world of computers and motorways. Paranoid Android lasts more than six minutes and consists of four different parts. Critics compared it with Bohemian Rhapsody by Queen from 1975. The album was praised as one of the best ever, and showed that a rock album could still be a work of art.
genres.listen: Paranoid Android changes time signature, with a section in 7/8. Listen to how quiet and hard sections alternate.

genres.name: Rage Against the Machine: The Battle of Los Angeles
genres.text: On 2 November 1999 The Battle of Los Angeles by Rage Against the Machine was released. The band mixed heavy rock guitars with rap and sang about injustice and power. The album went straight in at number 1 in America. Guitarist Tom Morello made his guitar sound like a scratching DJ, with effects pedals and all kinds of tricks. Guerrilla Radio won a Grammy. Soon afterwards the band split up.
genres.listen: In Testify, listen to Tom Morello's howling, squeaking sounds. That is not a turntable but a guitar.

genres.name: Radiohead: Kid A
genres.text: On 2 October 2000 Kid A by Radiohead was released. After the success of OK Computer, the band largely let go of guitars for electronics, drum machines and jazz horns. There were no singles and no videos. The album could be leaked and downloaded via Napster weeks before its release, and yet it went to number one in America. Many fans were at first bewildered, but it became one of the best-known albums of the decade.
genres.listen: In Everything in Its Right Place, Thom Yorke's voice is cut into pieces and distorted. Listen to the synthesizer that keeps playing the same chords.

genres.name: Muse: Plug In Baby
genres.text: In March 2001 Plug In Baby by Muse was released, a band from the English seaside town of Teignmouth. Singer and guitarist Matt Bellamy played fast runs that sounded like classical music, with a lot of effects. Muse carried on the line of progressive rock and Queen: big, dramatic and technical. In the years that followed they became one of the biggest stadium bands in Europe.
genres.listen: The guitar riff of Plug In Baby sounds like a fast run by Bach, but through a distorted guitar.

genres.name: The Strokes: Is This It
genres.text: On 30 July 2001 Is This It, the debut of The Strokes from New York, was released, first in Australia and later in Britain and America. The short, raw songs recalled The Velvet Underground and the punk of CBGB. After the attacks of 11 September, the band removed New York City Cops from the American CD. The album gave garage rock a fresh start and inspired many young guitar bands.
genres.listen: In Last Nite, listen to the two guitars, each playing its own tight pattern. The vocals sound deliberately distorted and dull, as if the singer is standing far away.

genres.name: Coldplay: The Scientist
genres.text: On 11 November 2002 The Scientist by Coldplay, from London, was released, from the album A Rush of Blood to the Head. It is a piano ballad: Chris Martin begins alone on piano and the band only comes in after the first chorus. In the video everything runs backwards, and Martin learned to sing the lyrics backwards. Coldplay grew into one of the biggest stadium bands of the twenty-first century.
genres.listen: Listen to the piano that carries the whole song. Only towards the end does the electric guitar join in.

genres.name: Linkin Park: Numb
genres.text: In September 2003 Numb by Linkin Park was released as a single, from the album Meteora. The band mixed metal with hip-hop and electronics: nu metal. Singer Chester Bennington sang and screamed, Mike Shinoda rapped and made beats. Numb is about someone who feels they are never good enough for others. It became one of the most streamed rock songs ever, even long after Bennington died in 2017.
genres.listen: Listen to the piano melody and the electronic beat under the guitars. Bennington sings the chorus almost screaming.

genres.name: The Killers: Mr. Brightside
genres.text: In June 2004 Hot Fuss, the first album by The Killers from Las Vegas, was released. They sounded British, with synthesizers and the energy of 1980s new wave. Mr. Brightside, about jealousy, became one of the best-known rock songs of the century. In Britain it stayed in the chart for years. Rock bands still scored worldwide hits, but there would be fewer and fewer of them.
genres.listen: Mr. Brightside has only one verse: after the chorus the song starts again with exactly the same words. Listen to how it still gets more and more exciting.

tracks.title: All These Things That I've Done

genres.name: Arcade Fire: Funeral
genres.text: On 14 September 2004 Funeral, the first album by Arcade Fire from Montreal in Canada, was released. The title refers to relatives of band members who died around that time. The large group played violin, accordion and xylophone as well as guitars. A glowing review from the music site Pitchfork quickly made the small album known. It showed that an indie band could also find a large audience through the internet.
genres.listen: In Wake Up, listen to how the whole band sings a wordless choir together. It sounds like a large audience singing along.

genres.name: Arctic Monkeys: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
genres.text: On 23 January 2006 the debut by Arctic Monkeys from Sheffield was released. The band gave away demo CDs at gigs, and fans put the songs on the internet. So the public already knew the songs before there was a record. In the first week more than 360,000 copies were sold, the fastest-selling debut in British history. Singer Alex Turner sang in his own accent about going out in his city.
genres.listen: In I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor, listen to how fast Alex Turner sings, in the Sheffield accent, about a night at the disco.

tracks.title: I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor

genres.name: MGMT: Oracular Spectacular
genres.text: On 2 October 2007 Oracular Spectacular, the debut of MGMT, was released, first as a download and in January 2008 on CD. Andrew VanWyngarden and Ben Goldwasser met at university. With producer Dave Fridmann they made psychedelic pop with synthesizers, falsetto vocals and dreamy lyrics. Time to Pretend, Electric Feel and Kids became festival hits. Psychedelia, forty years after Sgt. Pepper, sounded fresh again.
genres.listen: In Time to Pretend, listen to the bright synthesizer melody that keeps coming back. The lyrics mockingly dream of life as a rock star.

genres.name: Radiohead: In Rainbows
genres.text: On 10 October 2007 Radiohead put the album In Rainbows on the internet. The band no longer had a record company and let fans choose for themselves what to pay for the download, even nothing. The news went around the world. Only in December did the album also come out on CD. It showed that a band could distribute its music itself, at a time when CDs were selling less and less.
genres.listen: In 15 Step, listen to the rhythm of five beats per bar instead of the usual four, with electronic drums and handclaps.

genres.name: Kings of Leon: Sex on Fire
genres.text: In September 2008 Sex on Fire by Kings of Leon was released, three brothers and a cousin from the Followill family. They grew up in the American South and began with southern rock, the line of Lynyrd Skynyrd. Sex on Fire, from the album Only by the Night, became their first number one, in Britain, Ireland, Australia and Finland. After that, rock appeared less and less often at the top of the charts.
genres.listen: Listen to Caleb Followill's raw voice and the chiming guitar lick that carries on through the whole song.

genres.name: Mumford & Sons: Little Lion Man
genres.text: In the summer of 2009 Little Lion Man by Mumford & Sons, from London, was released, from the album Sigh No More. There is a banjo and an acoustic guitar, but the kick drum and the build-up come from stadium rock: folk rock on an arena scale. The album sold millions of copies. In the decade that followed, hip-hop, pop and dance took over the charts almost completely, and rock went quiet.
genres.listen: In Little Lion Man, listen to the banjo picking fast above the acoustic guitar, and how the kick drum pushes the song towards a big chorus.
